clue.text: Company receiving genuine anonymous warning

indicators.note: receiving means taking in, so the word for company opens up to hold the other two pieces

parts.note: a company is a firm; it opens up to take the rest inside
A = anonymous, the abbreviation used for an unnamed author

explanation.surface: A firm takes in a real tip-off from an unnamed source.
explanation.walkthrough: A for 'anonymous' is the abbreviation used for unsigned writing, worth banking. The surface suggests a whistleblower's tip; the answer is a much more literal warning.
explanation.definitionFit: A fire alarm is a device that raises a warning — the definition names the machine by its function, warning being what it exists to do.

clue.text: Score twice, like A Castle?

definitions.meaning: a score is twenty; this fragment doubles it
read as a word meaning resembling a fort, i.e. a castle, split into two parts that combine to spell the number

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether doubling a score makes a thing castle-like.
explanation.walkthrough: The capitals in 'A Castle' suggest a person's name, but the clue wants FORT plus the adjective ending -Y — castle-like, as the question mark concedes.
explanation.definitionFit: A score is twenty, so score twice is forty; and FORTY split as FORT-Y whimsically means fort-like, which is exactly what a castle is.

clue.text: French poet traumatised Vietnam veteran on film, reportedly

indicators.note: reportedly means as heard by report, so the film character's name is said aloud and entered with another spelling

parts.note: Rambo is Sylvester Stallone's traumatised veteran in First Blood

explanation.surface: A French poet is likened in name to a film's damaged Vietnam veteran.
explanation.walkthrough: Arthur Rimbaud and John Rambo are pronounced alike in English — a favourite crossword pairing of poet and action hero.
explanation.definitionFit: Arthur Rimbaud was the 19th-century French Symbolist poet who wrote A Season in Hell, so the definition points straight at him by class.

clue.text: American chap is spy

parts.note: an informal word for a well-mannered man, shortened from a longer, more formal one

explanation.surface: An American man turns out to be a spy.
explanation.walkthrough: A for American is a dictionary abbreviation worth banking; the rest is a chap being a GENT.
explanation.definitionFit: An agent here is a secret agent — someone spying for an intelligence service, not the estate or travel kind.

clue.text: Content of dustcart taken up to entice

indicators.note: in a down entry, taken up means the letters are read from the bottom of the grid upwards
the content of something is what sits inside it, so the letters lie within the words dustcart taken

parts.note: dus(TCARTTA)ken holds the letters; 'taken up' in this down entry reads them bottom to top

explanation.surface: What is in a dustcart gets lifted out to lure someone in.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer hides backwards across 'dustcart taken': lift TCARTTA up the grid and it spells ATTRACT. Fitting that a dustcart clue turns on its contents.
explanation.definitionFit: To attract is to entice — both mean to draw someone in, as a magnet or a bargain does.

clue.text: Sacking main guard after reshuffle

indicators.note: after a reshuffle the staff are in new positions, so the letters of main guard are put in a new order

explanation.surface: The main guard is sacked after a staff reshuffle.
explanation.walkthrough: A guard being sacked is the surface joke: reshuffle MAIN GUARD and the guards become the raiders they were meant to stop.
explanation.definitionFit: Sacking here is the pillaging sense — marauding troops sack towns — not dismissal from a job, which is what the surface wants you to hear.

clue.text: Possesses heroin and cannabis

parts.note: H is street shorthand for heroin, a crossword staple

explanation.surface: Someone is caught holding heroin and cannabis.
explanation.walkthrough: Every word of the surface stays inside the drugs world — possession charges and all — which is exactly why the simple HAS + H build is easy to miss.
explanation.definitionFit: Hash is short for hashish, the resin form of cannabis — an everyday informal synonym for the drug.

clue.text: Hard to consume chicken for non-believer

parts.note: H = hard, as on pencil grades

explanation.surface: It is hard for a non-believer to eat chicken.
explanation.walkthrough: Three short pieces in a row; the pencil-grade H = hard is the convention worth remembering.
explanation.definitionFit: A heathen is someone outside a (traditionally Christian) faith, so 'non-believer' is a plain synonym.

clue.text: Claims hob broken, which is chaotic

indicators.note: something broken is in pieces, so the letters of claims hob are put back together differently

explanation.surface: Someone complains the hob is broken, which leaves the kitchen in chaos.
explanation.walkthrough: A broken hob is a nicely domestic disaster for a word meaning total disorder.
explanation.definitionFit: Shambolic means chaotic or disorganised — from 'shambles', originally a butcher's slaughterhouse and hence any scene of mess.

clue.text: Mad brute altering rhythm?

indicators.note: altering means changing, so the letters of mad brute are set in a different order

explanation.surface: A raging brute changes the beat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mad' looks like the anagram signal but is actually fodder — 'altering' does the shuffling.
explanation.definitionFit: A drumbeat sets and carries a rhythm; the question mark concedes it is one particular rhythm-maker standing for rhythm in general.

clue.text: Anger a volatile US President

indicators.note: volatile means unstable and liable to change, so the letters of anger a will not stay put

explanation.surface: Anger makes a US President unpredictable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Volatile' is an instability word, a classic anagram signal — and anger makes apt fodder for a head of state.
explanation.definitionFit: Ronald Reagan, the actor turned politician, served as US president from 1981 to 1989 — the definition names the office and lets you pick the holder.

clue.text: Despot hurried into tryst regularly

indicators.note: into says the word for hurried goes inside the letters picked out of tryst
regularly means at even intervals, so every other letter of tryst is taken

parts.note: the odd letters of TrYsT, taken 'regularly'

explanation.surface: A despot rushes into a lovers' secret meeting now and then.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Regularly' is the instruction to take every other letter — one of the quieter signals, easy to mistake for surface. The picture is a runner interrupting a secret meeting; the answer is nothing so romantic.
explanation.definitionFit: A tyrant is a despot: both name an absolute ruler who governs oppressively, straight synonyms.

clue.text: A friend with addiction, briefly, in emirate

parts.note: bud is American slang for a friend, short for buddy

indicators.note: briefly means cut short, so the word for addiction loses its last letter

parts.note: a habit is an addiction, as in a drug habit

explanation.surface: A pal with a short-lived drug problem turns up in the Gulf.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads 'with addiction' as describing the friend, but it is a separate piece, cut short by 'briefly'.
explanation.definitionFit: Abu Dhabi is the largest of the seven United Arab Emirates and holds the federal capital.

clue.text: Large snake that gets one climbing?

parts.note: L = large, as on clothing labels
the adder is Britain's native venomous snake

explanation.surface: A large snake turns out to be what gets someone climbing.
explanation.walkthrough: A snake inside the answer to a climbing clue is a wink at Snakes and Ladders, where snakes send you down and ladders send you up.
explanation.definitionFit: A ladder is exactly what gets you climbing — the question mark flags a playful description doing duty as the definition.

clue.text: Virtue of watching Björn Again show, perhaps

parts.note: watching a show means being at it
Björn Again is an ABBA tribute band, so their gig is an example of a tribute show

explanation.surface: Seeing the ABBA tribute act Björn Again is presented as a virtue.
explanation.definitionFit: An attribute is a quality or characteristic, and a virtue is a good quality of that kind.

clue.text: Organise a contest with son in small cars

parts.note: to organise an event is to run it
a contest, especially in boxing, is a bout

explanation.surface: Someone arranges a race for a boy in little cars.
explanation.walkthrough: Four pieces chain together; only the boxing sense of 'contest' and the genealogist's S = son need spotting.
explanation.definitionFit: A runabout is a small light car for short local trips — a slightly dated word that survives happily in crosswords.

clue.text: Integral changes in shape

indicators.note: changes means alters, so the letters of integral are rearranged into a new word

explanation.surface: Something whole keeps changing its shape.
explanation.walkthrough: INTEGRAL and TRIANGLE are a classic anagram pair — the mathematical surface is a bonus.
explanation.definitionFit: A triangle is a three-sided shape — definition by class, with the maths-flavoured surface nudging you towards calculus instead of geometry.

clue.text: Wasted set point in hurry

indicators.note: wasted means ruined or squandered, so the letters of set point are broken up and rebuilt

explanation.surface: A tennis player squanders a set point and is told to hurry.
explanation.walkthrough: A tennis surface hides a driving phrase: waste the SET POINT and you are left with an instruction to accelerate.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Step on it' means hurry — from stepping on a car's accelerator, a whole-phrase idiom rather than a word-for-word match.

clue.text: Walk around official introduction

indicators.note: around says the word for walk goes round the short word for a match official

parts.note: a match official is the ref

explanation.surface: A referee strolls around making an official introduction.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Official' does double duty: it reads as an adjective in the surface, meaning formal, and works as a noun in the wordplay, meaning referee. That switch of part of speech is where the clue hides.
explanation.definitionFit: A preface is the introduction at the front of a book — 'pre-face' literally names what comes before the main text.

clue.text: NATO lie about providing protective cover

indicators.note: about means all over the place, so the letters of NATO lie are scattered and reset

explanation.surface: NATO tells lies about giving protective cover.
explanation.walkthrough: Geopolitical intrigue dissolves into anatomy once 'about' scrambles NATO LIE.
explanation.definitionFit: A toenail is the hard plate shielding the top of the toe — quite literally a protective cover for the digit.

clue.text: Announcement of oil in country

indicators.note: an announcement is spoken out, so the word for oil counts by its sound rather than its spelling

explanation.surface: News of an oil find breaks in a country.
explanation.walkthrough: GREASE said aloud gives the country — the same pun the musical Grease has traded on for decades.
explanation.definitionFit: Greece is a southern European country — a plain class definition; the letters simply arrive by ear rather than on the page.

clue.text: Loan the drunk something bad for them?

indicators.note: a drunk person staggers about, so the letters of loan the lurch into a new order

explanation.surface: Lending money to the drunk might do them harm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drunk' does double duty: it scrambles LOAN THE, and it is also the 'them' the definition points back at — a neat little loop.
explanation.definitionFit: Ethanol is the alcohol in drink, so for a drunk it is precisely the harmful substance — the question mark winks at the self-reference.

clue.text: Tell story about Blake Lively being nice

indicators.note: the word for fibbing goes about, around, the rearranged letters

parts.note: to tell a story is to fib, to lie

indicators.note: lively means bouncing about energetically, so the letters of Blake are shaken into a new order

explanation.surface: Gossip spreads a false tale about the actress Blake Lively being pleasant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lively' looks like the actress's surname, but it is the anagram signal on her first name; 'Tell story' gives the fib that goes 'about' the result.
explanation.definitionFit: Nice and likeable are synonyms, both describing a pleasant person who is easy to get on with.

clue.text: Try again: what is stuck in bottom?

indicators.note: stuck in means wedged inside, so the word for what goes into the word for bottom

explanation.surface: Someone asks what is stuck in their backside and tries again.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is courtroom language: a case tried again is reheard. 'Eh?' for 'what?' is a little interjection worth banking.
explanation.definitionFit: To rehear a case is to try it again in court — 'try' in the judicial sense of hearing a case, not of attempting something.

clue.text: Legendary brother beginning to raise flightless birds

indicators.note: the beginning to raise is its opening letter, so only that one letter is taken

explanation.surface: A legendary brother starts rearing flightless birds.
explanation.walkthrough: Remus was one of Rome's legendary twin founders, suckled by a wolf — which makes 'raise' a sly word to take a beginning from.
explanation.definitionFit: Remus is the brother of Romulus in the legend of Rome's founding, so 'legendary brother' defines him by example.

clue.text: A model upset Greek storyteller

indicators.note: upset in a down entry means turned upside down, so the joined letters of model and a read from the bottom

parts.note: POSE (to model, as for a portrait) turned upwards

explanation.surface: A model throws a tantrum at a Greek storyteller.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down entry 'upset' flips POSE on its head. The surface's difficult model is a red herring.
explanation.definitionFit: Aesop is the ancient Greek fabulist credited with the fables of the tortoise and the hare, so 'storyteller' fits him by example.

clue.text: Where you might need to go, some might say, in Pacific islands

indicators.note: some might say points to how a phrase is pronounced, so where you might need to go is spoken to give the letters

parts.words: Where you might need to go
parts.note: a person needing 'to go' is headed to a loo

explanation.surface: A traveller wonders where the toilets are on some Pacific islands.
explanation.walkthrough: Needing 'to go' is needing the loo; say 'to a loo' quickly and the island nation appears. 'Some might say' flags the deliberately loose pronunciation.
explanation.definitionFit: Tuvalu is a Pacific nation made up of nine low-lying islands, so the plural 'islands' fairly names the whole country.

clue.text: Rebuke beautiful Greek husband pinching millions

indicators.note: pinching means gripping tightly, so the beautiful Greek's name nips the letter for millions inside it

parts.note: Adonis, the byword for male beauty in Greek myth

explanation.surface: A beautiful Greek husband is rebuked for stealing millions.
explanation.walkthrough: ADONIS and H make the 'beautiful Greek husband', who then pinches M near the front: AD(M)ONISH.
explanation.definitionFit: To admonish someone is to rebuke them, though usually more in gentle warning than in anger — a close verb-for-verb synonym.

clue.text: Lake shimmered, somewhat

indicators.note: somewhat means only to some extent, so just part of shimmered is wanted

explanation.surface: A lake shimmered a little.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Somewhat' asks for only part of 'shimmered' — and a shimmering lake makes the surface picture-perfect.
explanation.definitionFit: A mere is a lake or pond — an old English word that survives in place names like Windermere and, of course, in crosswords.

clue.text: Receipt of disappointing news for rep?

definitions.meaning: the American term for the piece of paper you get after a shop purchase
read as a two-word sentence about a decline in what's being sold — grim news for whoever's selling it

explanation.surface: A sales rep receives disappointing news.
explanation.walkthrough: One phrase, two readings: the paper in the till, or sales taking a dive — which a sales rep would rather not hear about.
explanation.definitionFit: A sales slip is a receipt in American usage; reread as a sentence, sales that slip are exactly what a sales rep dreads.
